summary.text: A molecule or ion is chiral if it cannot be superposed on its mirror image by any combination of rotations, translations and some conformational changes.
A chiral molecule exists as two mirror-image stereoisomers called enantiomers, which have the same chemical properties except when reacting with other chiral compounds.
Chirality matters in biochemistry: organisms typically hold only one enantiomer of a chiral compound, so the effects of a drug's enantiomers can differ sharply.

facts.label: Most common source
facts.value: A carbon atom with four distinct groups attached

items.prompt: The word chirality comes from the Greek for "hand", and a hand is the classic example. Why?

options.label: Hands have five parts, like the groups around a stereocenter
Hands come in pairs, so chiral molecules form pairs of atoms
A hand can be rotated into place over its mirror image
A hand and its mirror image cannot be laid exactly over each other

items.explain: A hand is the canonical example of an object that cannot be superposed on its mirror image, which is what chirality means.

items.prompt: An organic molecule has exactly one carbon bonded to four different groups, and no other stereogenic carbon. What must be true of it?

options.label: It is chiral
It is achiral, since a single centre has no mirror
It is a meso compound
It is chiral only at low temperature

items.explain: An organic compound with only one stereogenic carbon is always chiral.

items.prompt: A molecule has several stereocenters, but they are arranged so that it can take a conformation with a plane of symmetry. Is it chiral?

options.label: Yes, since several stereocenters always make it chiral
Yes, but only in its conformation without symmetry
No, it is achiral and known as a meso compound
No, it is chiral only when it has one stereocenter

items.explain: A compound with multiple stereogenic carbons is typically, but not always, chiral; one that can take a conformation with a plane of symmetry is achiral and called a meso compound.

items.prompt: An organism feeds on a chiral compound. What is it likely to do with the compound's mirror-image form?

options.label: Use it just as well, since the chemistry is the same
Usually be unable to metabolise it
Turn it into the first form at once
Store it unchanged as a racemic mixture

items.explain: Living organisms typically hold only one enantiomer, so organisms that consume a chiral compound usually can metabolise only one of its enantiomers.

items.prompt: A chemist mixes equal parts of the two enantiomers of a compound. How does the mixture compare with a pure enantiomer?

options.label: It behaves exactly like either pure form
It differs only in its optical activity
It is a single new molecule joined together
It differs chemically and physically from the pure forms

items.explain: A racemic mixture, equal parts of both enantiomers, differs chemically and physically from the pure enantiomers.

items.prompt: At room temperature butane is considered achiral, even though some of its conformers are chiral. Why?

options.label: Rotation about its central bond rapidly interconverts the mirror-image forms
Its twisted conformers do not actually exist
Its mirror-image forms are too alike to tell apart
It is too small to have any real shape

items.explain: Rotation about the central C–C bond rapidly interconverts the enantiomeric conformers, so the molecule is considered achiral at room temperature.
